lesson.title: Where Files Live: Understanding File Paths
lesson.summary: A file path is a string telling the operating system exactly where a file is, either relative to the current folder or absolute from the filesystem root, and because backslashes double as Python's escape character, an ordinary string can silently mangle a Windows style path unless it is written as a raw string.
lesson.body:
Every call to `open()` needs to know exactly which file on the entire computer you mean, and that information is carried by a file path, a string that describes where a file lives. Because a path is just a string, everything covered about the string type still applies: paths can be built, sliced, checked with `in`, and formatted like any other text, but that same flexibility means a path string can also be written incorrectly in ways that are easy to miss.

There are two broad kinds of paths. A relative path, like `"greeting.txt"` or `"data/scores.txt"`, is interpreted relative to the current working directory, essentially the folder your program is considered to be running from, which can change depending on how the program was started. An absolute path spells out the complete location starting from the root of the filesystem, something like `"/Users/name/project/greeting.txt"` on Mac and Linux, or `"C:\Users\name\project\greeting.txt"` on Windows. Relative paths are shorter and more portable between computers, since they do not depend on any one person's folder structure, but they only work correctly if the program is run from the folder you expect.

Windows paths traditionally use backslashes to separate folders, while Mac and Linux use forward slashes, and this difference collides badly with how Python reads string literals, because backslash is also Python's escape character. Writing a Windows style path as an ordinary string can silently produce something completely different from what you intended, since Python looks for recognized escape sequences like `\n` for newline or `\t` for tab anywhere a backslash appears, whether you meant it as an escape or not.

```python
bad_path = "C:\notes\new_file.txt"
good_path = r"C:\notes\new_file.txt"

print(bad_path)
print(good_path)
```

```python
C:
otes
ew_file.txt
C:\notes\new_file.txt
```

Read `bad_path` the way Python's interpreter reads it, one backslash at a time. `\n` inside `\notes` is not "backslash then the letter n," it is the recognized escape sequence for a newline character, so that word becomes a newline followed by the letters `otes`. The same thing happens again inside `\new_file.txt`, where `\n` becomes another newline, leaving `ew_file.txt` after it. The string Python actually built has real line breaks buried inside it, which is exactly why `print(bad_path)` shows three broken lines instead of one sensible path, and why trying to `open()` a path like this would almost certainly fail to find the file you meant.

`good_path` fixes this with a raw string, written with an `r` immediately before the opening quote: `r"C:\notes\new_file.txt"`. Inside a raw string, Python turns off escape sequence processing entirely, so every backslash is treated as a literal backslash character, nothing more. Printing `good_path` shows the path exactly as it was typed, all on one line, with the backslashes intact. The safest habits for writing paths in Python are to use raw strings for anything containing backslashes, to use forward slashes when you can since Python accepts them even on Windows, or, for serious path handling in larger programs, to reach for the `pathlib` module, which builds and joins paths correctly for whatever operating system the code happens to be running on.
